text: Cost is one half of running an AI service responsibly. Monitoring what it's actually doing is the other half, and it closes out this chapter.

Monitoring here covers three layers. Operational metrics — token usage, latency, run success rate. Evaluation metrics — coherence, fluency, groundedness, scored on sampled production traffic. And tracing, which captures the full execution path of a single request, end to end.
The Monitor tab brings all of this into one dashboard: summary cards at the top, with token usage, run success, and error-rate charts below them, filterable by time range.

A few thresholds are worth knowing by heart. Latency above ten seconds usually signals throttling, a slow tool call, or a network issue. A success rate below ninety-five percent is worth investigating directly. And a sudden token usage spike is often a verbose prompt or a response with no length limit.
The Monitor settings panel is where you turn each of these on: operational metrics, continuous evaluation, scheduled evaluation, red team scans, and alerts, all configured from one place.

Recurring evaluations are what make this sustainable. Instead of manually checking quality now and then, a recurring evaluation samples live traffic or runs on a fixed schedule, so quality drift gets caught automatically, without anyone having to remember to look.
That wraps up working with Azure AI services directly. From here, the course moves one layer down, into the cloud infrastructure — compute, storage, networking — that these services actually run on.
